analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for older workers to win age discrimination lawsuits.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to make age discrimination cases easier to win — backed by 7 cosponsors from both parties — sat in the Senate labor committee without a hearing or vote until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2009 Supreme Court ruling made it much harder to win age discrimination cases, this bill would have restored the easier standard: a worker would only need to show age was one motivating factor in an employer's decision, not the sole cause. It would apply the same easier standard to disability and other discrimination claims. The bill also limits damages when an employer proves it would have made the same decision regardless of age.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and over who believe they were fired, demoted, or passed over because of age would no longer have to prove age was the deciding factor — only one motivating factor among others — making age discrimination cases much easier to win. Workers with disabilities, federal employees, and people claiming retaliation would get the same easier standard, and all workers could use any admissible evidence to make their case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers over 40 and workers with disabilities

how_it_helps.text: Workers would only need to show that age was a motivating factor in an adverse employment decision, rather than proving under the Supreme Court's 2009 Gross ruling that age was the deciding cause — a burden the bill's own findings say has 'significantly narrowed' protections.
The bill states workers may rely on any type of admissible evidence and are not required to prove age or retaliation was the sole cause of the employer's action.
The same easier standard would apply to disability discrimination claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act, Rehabilitation Act claims, and discrimination claims by federal employees.

To limit the cost to employers, if the employer proves it would have made the same decision without the discriminatory motive, the worker could get a declaration, an injunction, and attorney fees but no damages, reinstatement, or back pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those with large older workforces, would face easier-to-win discrimination lawsuits, more settlements, and attorney fee awards in cases they lose, though the bill caps remedies when the employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway.

drawbacks.text: The motivating-factor standard lets a worker win even when age was only one of several reasons for the decision, which employers argue exposes them to liability for legitimate business decisions made for a mix of reasons.
The bill would apply retroactively to all claims pending on or after enactment, changing the rules mid-litigation for cases already in court.

In mixed-motive cases where the employer proves the same decision would have been made anyway, the worker gets no damages, reinstatement, or back pay — only a declaration, an injunction, and limited attorney fees — so some winning workers would receive little meaningful relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to older workers and workers with disabilities is substantial: the 2009 Gross ruling made age cases among the hardest discrimination claims to win, and this bill would have restored the standard Congress set for other civil rights claims in 1991. The main cost falls on employers in the form of more litigation, but the bill was deliberately designed to limit that cost — if an employer proves the outcome would have been the same without discrimination, the worker gets no money damages. That compromise structure, plus bipartisan sponsorship that included conservative Republicans like Grassley, suggests the design was defensible; the bill's death without even a committee hearing left the worker-friendly change unmade.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 8, 2015 and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill sat in committee until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The bill would have let workers prove age discrimination by showing age was a motivating factor rather than the sole cause, reversing the standard set by the Supreme Court in Gross v. FBL Financial Services.

Sponsorship crossed party and ideological lines: Republican sponsor Mark Kirk joined conservative Republican Chuck Grassley and Collins alongside Democrats Casey, Leahy, and Coons, with 7 cosponsors total (4 Democrats, 3 Republicans).
The bill also applied the easier motivating-factor standard to disability discrimination claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act and to claims by federal employees.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing age and disability discrimination claims came out ahead: the harder 'but-for' standard from the 2009 Gross ruling stays in place, and no other changes to the law were made.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split evenly between the parties — 4 Senate Democrats and 4 Senate Republicans, including conservative Republican Chuck Grassley and liberal Democrat Patrick Leahy — and the bill died in committee without a vote, so no party-line floor fight ever happened.

industries.industry: Employers with 20 or more workers (covered by the age discrimination law)
industries.note: The bill would make age and disability discrimination cases substantially easier for workers to win by replacing the strict 'but-for' causation standard with a 'motivating factor' standard, increasing litigation exposure and settlement costs.
The bill would expand the pool of viable discrimination claims, making it easier for plaintiffs' attorneys to take age and disability cases on contingency.
